claims.claim: Temperature fundamentally limits mosquito ranges and persistence through its influence on mosquito survival, development, and reproductive rates.
claims.source: Temperature fundamentally limits mosquito ranges and persistence through its influence on mosquito survival, development, and reproductive rates.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of mosquito biology.

claims.claim: The precise aspects of temperature that determine mosquito population limits remain unclear.
claims.source: However, the precise aspects of temperature that determine these limits remain unclear (Christophers, 1960; Yang et al., 2009; Brady et al., 2013; Shapiro et al., 2017; Tesla et al., 2018; Shocket et al., 2018; Mordecai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of knowledge gaps supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Temperature averages, variability, extremes, and interactions among these factors all impact ectotherm fitness.
claims.source: Temperature averages, variability, extremes, and interactions among these factors all impact ectotherm fitness (Nene et al., 2007; Lambrechts et al., 2011; Bozinovic et al., 2011; Kingsolver et al., 2013; Paaijmans et al., 2013; Blanford et al., 2013; Dowd et al., 2015; Buckley and Huey, 2016; Ma et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: The temperature variable that most strongly constrains persistence for a particular mosquito population will likely vary based on breeding and resting habitat preferences and by location.
claims.source: The temperature variable that most strongly constrains persistence for a particular mosquito population will likely vary based on breeding and resting habitat preferences and by location, as thermal regimes can differ greatly between water sources used for oviposition, between indoor and outdoor environments, and by latitude and altitude (Paaijmans et al., 2008; Paaijmans et al., 2010; Paaijmans and Thomas, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reflects inference about context-dependent effects.

claims.claim: Changes in diurnal temperature variation may impose strong selection on East African An. arabiensis populations that primarily rest outdoors.
claims.source: For example, changes in diurnal temperature variation may impose strong selection on East African An. arabiensis populations that primarily rest outdoors (Githeko et al., 1996), but have less impact on An. gambiae s.s and An. funestus populations that primarily rest indoors, where temperatures vary less drastically (Bødker et al., 2003; Minakawa et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mosquito behavior and microclimate.

claims.claim: Maximum annual temperature has been identified as the strongest driver of species extinctions out of 19 WorldClim Bioclimatic variables.
claims.source: Based on evidence from other arthropod species, maximum annual temperature has been identified as the strongest driver of species extinctions (out of the 19 WorldClim Bioclimatic variables; Román-Palacios and Wiens, 2020), thus changes in maximum temperatures may exert the strongest selection pressure on mosquito populations near their warm range limits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Román-Palacios and Wiens, 2020.

claims.claim: Changes in maximum temperatures may exert the strongest selection pressure on mosquito populations near their warm range limits.
claims.source: Based on evidence from other arthropod species, maximum annual temperature has been identified as the strongest driver of species extinctions (out of the 19 WorldClim Bioclimatic variables; Román-Palacios and Wiens, 2020), thus changes in maximum temperatures may exert the strongest selection pressure on mosquito populations near their warm range limits.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on evidence from other arthropod species.

claims.claim: Most temperature-trait responses are studied under constant temperatures.
claims.source: As most temperature – trait responses are studied under constant temperatures (Deutsch et al., 2008; Angilletta, 2009; Paaijmans et al., 2013; Vasseur et al., 2014; Dowd et al., 2015; Buckley and Huey, 2016), we consider mosquito responses to increases in mean temperature as a focal example.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Mosquito life history traits with the lowest critical thermal maxima will experience the strongest thermal selection.
claims.source: We hypothesize that mosquito life history traits with the lowest critical thermal maxima will experience the strongest thermal selection as environmental temperatures that exceed this limit have especially strong negative impacts on ectotherm fitness (Deutsch et al., 2008; Kingsolver et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited theoretical and empirical work.

claims.claim: For several mosquito vector species, adult lifespan and fecundity have the lowest critical thermal maxima, suggesting thermal selection may be strongest on the adult life stage.
claims.source: For several mosquito vector species, these traits are adult lifespan and fecundity, suggesting thermal selection may be strongest on the adult life stage (Figure 1; reviewed in Mordecai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review paper and reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: Whether life history traits with the lowest critical thermal maxima also pose the strongest constraints on mosquito fitness and persistence at high temperatures remains poorly understood.
claims.source: However, whether these life history traits also pose the strongest constraints on mosquito fitness and persistence at high temperatures remains poorly understood because prior work has largely focused on mosquito traits related to disease transmission during the activity season, but there may be additional traits that help mosquitoes tolerate climate extremes (e.g. diapause, aestivation).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of knowledge gaps based on literature review.

claims.claim: Populations can persist only when their maximum sustainable evolutionary rate exceeds the required rate of evolution dictated by the environment.
claims.source: Populations can persist only when their maximum sustainable evolutionary rate exceeds the required rate of evolution dictated by the environment (Bell and Gonzalez, 2009; Hoffmann and Sgrò, 2011; Gomulkiewicz and Shaw, 2013; Gonzalez et al., 2013; Carlson et al., 2014; Bell, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical papers on evolutionary rescue.

claims.claim: Evolutionary rescue models are well-suited to estimating the potential for thermal adaptation in response to climate warming.
claims.source: As these models track population responses to sustained, directional environmental change, they are well-suited to estimating the potential for thermal adaptation in response to climate warming (Huey and Kingsolver, 1993; Bürger and Lynch, 1995; Chevin et al., 2010; Bay et al., 2017; Cotto et al., 2017; Diniz‐Filho et al., 2019), and have provided valuable estimates of climate adaptation potential across a range of taxa (Gienapp et al., 2013; Bush et al., 2016; Cotto et al., 2017; Diniz‐Filho et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical papers.

claims.claim: Short generation times enable rapid evolutionary responses.
claims.source: Short generation times enable rapid evolutionary responses (Lynch and Lande, 1993; Bürger and Lynch, 1995), and high intrinsic population growth rates reduce the chance of extinction prior to adaptation (Bürger and Lynch, 1995; Orr and Unckless, 2008; Gomulkiewicz and Houle, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical population genetics papers.

claims.claim: High intrinsic population growth rates reduce the chance of extinction prior to adaptation.
claims.source: Short generation times enable rapid evolutionary responses (Lynch and Lande, 1993; Bürger and Lynch, 1995), and high intrinsic population growth rates reduce the chance of extinction prior to adaptation (Bürger and Lynch, 1995; Orr and Unckless, 2008; Gomulkiewicz and Houle, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical papers.

claims.claim: Precise demographic estimates for mosquitoes under natural conditions are unavailable for most species.
claims.source: The generally rapid life cycles and large population sizes of mosquitoes favor rapid evolution, but precise demographic estimates under natural conditions are unavailable for most species (but see Appendix 2—table 1 for growth rates and generation times for Ae. aegypti, Anopheles spp., and Cx. pipiens) and will vary with biotic and abiotic conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of data availability based on literature review.

claims.claim: High estimates of mosquito lifespans are approximately 3 months.
claims.source: However, even high estimates of mosquito lifespans of approximately 3 months (Macdonald, 1952; Nayar and Sauerman, 1971; Papadopoulos et al., 2016; Joubert et al., 2016) are on par with or well below those of other species that have already demonstrated evolutionary responses to climate change (e.g. Drosophila subobscura, Rodríguez-Trelles and Rodríguez, 1998; Balanyá et al., 2006; Tamiaschirus hudsonicus, Réale et al., 2003; Brassica rapa, Franks et al., 2007, several bird species, Gienapp et al., 2007; Cepaea nemoralis, Ożgo and Schilthuizen, 2012; Oncorhynchus gorbuscha, Kovach et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: High intrinsic population growth rates of 0.19–0.38 per generation have been calculated for several major vector species.
claims.source: Further, high intrinsic population growth rates (r) of 0.19–0.38 per generation have been calculated for several major vector species (Appendix 2—table 1, Equation 1, Figure 1; Amarasekare and Savage, 2012; Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2020) and census population size estimates on the order of 1,000–10,000 individuals have been found across studies of varying mosquito species and settings (Touré et al., 1998; Lehmann et al., 1998; Maciel-de-Freitas et al., 2008; Neira et al., 2014; Le Goff et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies and data in appendices.

claims.claim: Census population size estimates on the order of 1,000–10,000 individuals have been found across studies of varying mosquito species and settings.
claims.source: Further, high intrinsic population growth rates (r) of 0.19–0.38 per generation have been calculated for several major vector species (Appendix 2—table 1, Equation 1, Figure 1; Amarasekare and Savage, 2012; Johnson et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2017; Shocket et al., 2020) and census population size estimates on the order of 1,000–10,000 individuals have been found across studies of varying mosquito species and settings (Touré et al., 1998; Lehmann et al., 1998; Maciel-de-Freitas et al., 2008; Neira et al., 2014; Le Goff et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: A Drosophila modeling study showed that growth rates and population sizes in the range of mosquito values facilitated population persistence for over 300 generations under heat-knockdown selection.
claims.source: Placing these mosquito results in context, a Drosophila modeling study showed that growth rates and population sizes in this range facilitated population persistence for over 300 generations under heat-knockdown selection (Willi and Hoffmann, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Willi and Hoffmann, 2009.

claims.claim: Mosquito demographic characteristics favor thermal adaptation.
claims.source: Mosquito demographic characteristics therefore favor thermal adaptation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the synthesis of demographic data and comparison with other species.

claims.claim: Higher genetically based variance in a trait results in higher rates of phenotypic evolution.
claims.source: Higher genetically based variance in a trait results in higher rates of phenotypic evolution (Lande, 1976).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lande, 1976, a foundational paper in quantitative genetics.

claims.claim: No studies have measured within-population variation in mosquito thermal tolerance.
claims.source: While no studies (to our knowledge) have measured within-population variation in mosquito thermal tolerance, several studies have investigated variation between populations (Mogi, 1992; Reisen, 1995; Dodson et al., 2012; Vorhees et al., 2013; Ruybal et al., 2016; Chu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the literature indicating a knowledge gap.

claims.claim: Several studies have investigated variation in thermal tolerance between mosquito populations.
claims.source: While no studies (to our knowledge) have measured within-population variation in mosquito thermal tolerance, several studies have investigated variation between populations (Mogi, 1992; Reisen, 1995; Dodson et al., 2012; Vorhees et al., 2013; Ruybal et al., 2016; Chu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Studies of between-population variation in mosquito thermal tolerance find genetically based, but often trait-specific variation that did not always clearly support local thermal adaptation.
claims.source: Overall, these studies find genetically based, but often trait-specific variation that did not always clearly support local thermal adaptation (i.e. a correlation between trait values and local climatic conditions; Appendix 3—table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from multiple studies cited in the text and appendix.

claims.claim: Upper thermal limits of mosquito respiration and survival after heat shock were positively correlated with the temperature of origin for Cx. tarsalis and An. gambiae, respectively.
claims.source: For example, upper thermal limits of mosquito respiration and survival after heat shock were positively correlated with the temperature of origin for Cx. tarsalis and An. gambiae, respectively (Rocca et al., 2009; Vorhees et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two empirical studies.

claims.claim: Several studies have found thermal tolerance varying in the opposite direction from local adaptation expectations, or found minimal or no variation in thermal responses between populations.
claims.source: However, several other studies have found the opposite pattern (Ruybal et al., 2016), found minimal or no variation in thermal responses between populations (Dodson et al., 2012; Mogi, 1992), or found that certain populations had uniformly higher or lower trait performance at all experimental temperatures independent of their climate of origin (Ruybal et al., 2016; Reisen, 1995; Chu et al., 2019; Dodson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Mosquito populations do sometimes vary in their thermal performance, but there is no clear evidence for existing local thermal adaptation across temperature gradients of similar magnitude to those predicted by climate change.
claims.source: Taken together, mosquito populations do sometimes vary in their thermal performance, but there is no clear evidence for existing local thermal adaptation across temperature gradients of similar magnitude to those predicted by climate change over the next several decades.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the review of multiple studies.

claims.claim: The lack of clear evidence for local thermal adaptation may suggest either barriers to thermal adaptation or relatively weak selection on thermal performance.
claims.source: This may suggest either barriers to thermal adaptation or relatively weak selection on thermal performance (see 'Strength of selection' section).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the evidence.

claims.claim: The lack of within-population sampling and/or idiosyncratic, trait-specific temperature relationships may have obscured true patterns of local adaptation.
claims.source: However, the lack of within-population sampling and/or idiosyncratic, trait-specific temperature relationships may have obscured true patterns of local adaptation (Bradshaw et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of clear patterns, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: There are no estimates of the heritability of trait thermal tolerance for mosquitoes.
claims.source: To our knowledge, there are no estimates of the heritability of trait thermal tolerance for mosquitoes.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the literature indicating a knowledge gap.

claims.claim: Evolutionary theory and empirical work in other ectotherm taxa suggest that thermal tolerance heritability is generally low.
claims.source: However, evolutionary theory and empirical work in other ectotherm taxa suggest that thermal tolerance heritability is generally low.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on evolutionary theory and empirical work in other taxa.

claims.claim: Highly polygenic, complex, or environmentally-dependent traits typically have low heritability.
claims.source: In particular, highly polygenic, complex, or environmentally-dependent traits—as expected for thermal tolerances—typically have low heritability (Bay et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bay et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of heritability data for upper thermal limits in Drosophila resulted in an overall estimate of 0.28.
claims.source: Supporting this expectation, a meta-analysis of heritability data for upper thermal limits in Drosophila resulted in an overall estimate of 0.28 (i.e. 28% of the populations phenotypic variance is due to genetic variance; Diamond, 2017), which is similar to heritability estimates for other Drosophila life history traits (average h2 = 0.26; Roff and Mousseau, 1987, Mousseau and Roff, 1987) and indicates moderately low heritability (but see Jenkins and Hoffmann, 1994, h2 = 0.5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analysis and empirical studies.

claims.claim: Recent evidence suggests Drosophila can rapidly adapt to novel temperatures through multiple, alternative genetic pathways that lead to similar increases in thermal tolerance.
claims.source: However, more recent evidence suggests Drosophila can rapidly adapt to novel temperatures through multiple, alternative genetic pathways that lead to similar increases in thermal tolerance (i.e. 'genetic redundancy'), challenging the notion that highly polygenic traits have low heritability (Barghi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barghi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Uncertainty surrounding the ecological relevance of laboratory measurements of insect thermal tolerance limits our understanding of thermal tolerance trait heritability in mosquitoes.
claims.source: In general, uncertainty surrounding the ecological relevance of laboratory measurements of insect thermal tolerance (Terblanche et al., 2007; Chown et al., 2009; Mitchell and Hoffmann, 2010) and the divergent evolutionary histories of Drosopholids and mosquitoes limit our understanding of thermal tolerance trait heritability in mosquitoes.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of limitations in extrapolating from Drosophila to mosquitoes, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Stronger natural selection would lead to faster adaptive responses for heritable traits, despite causing high initial mortality.
claims.source: For heritable traits, stronger natural selection—the differential survival or reproduction of mosquitoes with different trait values—would lead to faster adaptive responses, despite causing high initial mortality (Box 1; Lynch and Lande, 1993; Hartl and Clark, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical population genetics texts.

claims.claim: Upper thermal limits for adult and larval survival are as low as 32–38°C.
claims.source: Upper thermal limits for adult and larval survival are as low as 32–38°C (reviewed in Mordecai et al., 2019), which many mosquito populations—particularly those in the tropics—already experience and will increasingly face in a warming climate (Deutsch et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to a review paper and an empirical study.

claims.claim: Many mosquito populations, particularly those in the tropics, already experience temperatures of 32–38°C and will increasingly face these temperatures in a warming climate.
claims.source: Upper thermal limits for adult and larval survival are as low as 32–38°C (reviewed in Mordecai et al., 2019), which many mosquito populations—particularly those in the tropics—already experience and will increasingly face in a warming climate (Deutsch et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reflects inference about climate change impacts.

claims.claim: Steep declines in survival between thermal optima and critical limits have been observed across mosquito species.
claims.source: Further, steep declines in survival between thermal optima and critical limits have been observed across mosquito species (Focks et al., 1993; Alto and Juliano, 2001; Kamimura et al., 2002; Delatte et al., 2009; Muturi et al., 2011; Mordecai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: High selection pressure may facilitate mosquito adaptation, provided that heritable variation in trait thermal tolerance exists.
claims.source: This high selection pressure may facilitate mosquito adaptation, provided that heritable variation in trait thermal tolerance exists.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary theory.

claims.claim: Phenotypic plasticity provides an alternative mechanism for coping with climate change that is more rapid than evolutionary adaptation.
claims.source: Phenotypic plasticity—the ability of individual genotypes to produce varying phenotypes based on the environment (West-Eberhard, 2003)—provides an alternative mechanism for coping with climate change that is more rapid than evolutionary adaptation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established ecological and evolutionary theory, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Plasticity may ultimately inhibit population persistence under long-term directional change because it impedes natural selection on genetically based variation.
claims.source: However, because plasticity impedes natural selection on genetically based variation, it may ultimately inhibit population persistence under long-term directional change (Gienapp et al., 2008; Whitman and Agrawal, 2009; Chevin et al., 2010; Chevin et al., 2013; Merilä and Hendry, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and review papers.

claims.claim: Potentially important plastic responses in mosquitoes include changes in activity patterns, biting behavior, microhabitat selection, thermal acclimation, and initiation of dormancy.
claims.source: For mosquitoes, potentially important plastic responses include changes in activity patterns, biting behavior, or microhabitat selection, thermal acclimation, and initiation of dormancy, as reviewed below (and see Appendix 3—table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about potential mechanisms based on literature review.

claims.claim: The capacity for plastic responses to increase thermal tolerance, their potential fitness costs, and how these plastic responses might interact with evolutionary adaptation remain poorly understood.
claims.source: Overall, mosquitoes possess a variety of potential plastic responses, but the capacity for these responses to increase thermal tolerance, their potential fitness costs, and how these plastic responses might interact with the process of evolutionary adaptation remain poorly understood.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of knowledge gaps based on literature review.

claims.claim: In laboratory thermal preference studies, Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex spp. have demonstrated behavioral avoidance of high temperatures when exposed to a thermal gradient.
claims.source: In laboratory thermal preference studies, Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex spp. have demonstrated behavioral avoidance of high temperatures when exposed to a thermal gradient (Thomson, 1938; Blanford et al., 2009; Verhulst et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Several studies have shown shifts in the biting time or habitat selection of mosquitoes, particularly An. gambiae, seasonally or in response to insecticide spraying.
claims.source: In natural settings, several studies have shown shifts in the biting time or habitat selection of mosquitoes, particularly An. gambiae, seasonally or in response to insecticide spraying (Taylor, 1975; Reisen and Aslamkhan, 1978; Voorham, 2002; Pates and Curtis, 2005; Manda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Studies have found increasing usage of underground or shaded oviposition sites that was correlated with increasing temperature in Ae. aegypti.
claims.source: While such behavioral shifts have not been conclusively linked to temperature, studies have found increasing usage of underground or shaded oviposition sites that was correlated with increasing temperature, and not associated with change in habitat availability or accompanied by genetic differentiation (Ae. aegypti, Somers et al., 2011; Chadee and Martinez, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Larvae in permafrost regions were observed to rest in deeper, cooler pond water when surface water temperatures became exceptionally high.
claims.source: Similarly, larvae in permafrost regions were observed to rest in deeper, cooler pond water when surface water temperatures became exceptionally high (Ae. communis, a non-vector species; Haufe and Burgess, 1956).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claims.claim: Evidence for mosquito behavioral thermoregulation more generally remains limited.
claims.source: Seeking out and accessing cooler microclimates may buffer mosquitoes from warm temperature extremes, reducing mortality and decreasing the strength of selection. However, evidence for mosquito behavioral thermoregulation more generally remains limited (Paaijmans and Thomas, 2011; Waldock et al., 2013), and trade-offs in resource acquisition from restricted foraging and activity time, and a lack of readily available cooler microhabitats would constrain this behavior (Angilletta, 2009; Sears et al., 2016; Huey and Kingsolver, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by citations.

claims.claim: Trade-offs in resource acquisition from restricted foraging and activity time, and a lack of readily available cooler microhabitats would constrain behavioral thermoregulation.
claims.source: Seeking out and accessing cooler microclimates may buffer mosquitoes from warm temperature extremes, reducing mortality and decreasing the strength of selection. However, evidence for mosquito behavioral thermoregulation more generally remains limited (Paaijmans and Thomas, 2011; Waldock et al., 2013), and trade-offs in resource acquisition from restricted foraging and activity time, and a lack of readily available cooler microhabitats would constrain this behavior (Angilletta, 2009; Sears et al., 2016; Huey and Kingsolver, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on ecological theory, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Increases in thermal tolerance after exposure to warmer temperatures during development have been documented in several mosquito species.
claims.source: Increases in thermal tolerance after exposure to warmer temperatures during development—a form of thermal acclimation—have been documented in several mosquito species (An. albimanus, Benedict et al., 1991; An. arabiensis and An. funestus, Lyons et al., 2012; Cx. pipiens, Gray, 2013; Ae. aegypti, Sivan et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Increases in thermal limits from acclimation were typically minimal, suggesting a limited capacity for thermal acclimation to reduce mortality at high temperatures.
claims.source: However, increases in thermal limits were typically minimal, suggesting a limited capacity for thermal acclimation to reduce mortality at high temperatures and enable population persistence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the magnitude of observed effects in cited studies.

claims.claim: Critical thermal limits of respirometry, motor function, or survival increased by less than 2°C for populations developing in 5°C warmer environments.
claims.source: For example, the critical thermal limits of respirometry, motor function, or survival increased by less than 2°C for populations developing in 5°C warmer environments (Benedict et al., 1991; Lyons et al., 2012; Gray, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Critical thermal maxima varied minimally with acclimation temperatures across a diverse range of over 200 ectotherm species.
claims.source: Similarly, critical thermal maxima varied minimally with acclimation temperatures across a diverse range of over 200 ectotherm species (Gunderson and Stillman, 2015; Somero et al., 2016; Heerwaarden et al., 2016; Rohr et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analyses and review papers.

claims.claim: Dormancy has been demonstrated in all major vector species.
claims.source: Temporarily unfavorable environmental conditions could be overcome through dormancy—the interruption or reduction of metabolic activity through diapause or quiescence—a response that has been demonstrated in all major vector species (reviewed in Diniz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review paper.

claims.claim: Dry-season dormancy is likely one mechanism enabling An. gambiae and An. coluzzi to persist during the 3- to 6-month long dry season in the Sahel.
claims.source: Dry-season dormancy (i.e. aestivation) is likely one mechanism enabling An. gambiae and An. coluzzi to persist during the 3- to 6-month long dry season in the Sahel, as evidenced by very low population sizes during the dry season followed by rapid increases after the first rain (Lehmann et al., 2010; Lehmann et al., 2014; Adamou et al., 2011; Yaro et al., 2012; Dao et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: There are no known examples of dormancy mechanisms in ectotherms that respond solely to high temperatures.
claims.source: However, there are no known examples of dormancy mechanisms in ectotherms that respond solely to high temperatures, thus this may be an unlikely response for mosquitoes, particularly tropical species facing warming temperatures in humid environments.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the literature and inference about mosquito responses.

claims.claim: Environmental sensitivity of selection refers to how the optimum phenotype shifts with changes in the environment.
claims.source: Environmental sensitivity of selection refers to how the optimum phenotype shifts with changes in the environment and is typically measured as the slope of the relationship between the optimal trait value and the environmental variable (e.g. the rate of change in the optimal upper thermal limit of adult life span against maximum summer temperature; Figure 1; Chevin et al., 2010, Chevin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to theoretical papers.

claims.claim: For mosquitoes, the environmental sensitivity of trait thermal tolerance has not been empirically measured.
claims.source: For mosquitoes, as for nearly all other organisms, the environmental sensitivity of trait thermal tolerance has not been empirically measured (Chevin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the literature indicating a knowledge gap, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Across mosquito populations and species, upper thermal limits for most mosquito life history traits were less variable than lower thermal limits and optima.
claims.source: However, across mosquito populations (Lyons et al., 2012; Vorhees et al., 2013) and species (Mordecai et al., 2019), upper thermal limits for most mosquito life history traits were less variable than lower thermal limits and optima.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: The pattern of less variable upper thermal limits may reflect evolutionary constraints on upper thermal tolerance.
claims.source: These patterns could reflect strong environmental sensitivity on lower thermal tolerance, intermediate sensitivity for the optimum, and weak sensitivity on upper thermal tolerance. However, it may more likely reflect evolutionary constraints on upper thermal tolerance (Kellermann et al., 2012; Hoffmann et al., 2013), or result from competing selection pressures, greater metabolic costs of heat versus cold tolerance, genetic constraints, or gene flow hindering thermal adaptation (Angilletta, 2009; Kristensen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to theoretical and empirical papers.

claims.claim: Projections of global mean annual surface temperatures in 2100 vary by over 3°C depending on the future climate scenario.
claims.source: Rates of environmental change will vary based on the specific temperature variable being considered (e.g. mean temperature of the hottest month or quarter, maximum temperature in the dry season, etc.), and depend on climate policy: projections of global mean annual surface temperatures in 2100 vary by over 3°C depending on the future climate scenario (Collins et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an IPCC report.

claims.claim: Greater warming is projected for higher latitudes.
claims.source: However, while greater warming is projected for higher latitudes (IPCC, 2007), faster rates of adaptation may be necessary for tropical mosquito populations that already experience environmental temperatures close to their thermal optima and may experience large fitness costs under additional warming in the absence of adaptation (Deutsch et al., 2008; Somero, 2010; Ryan et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an IPCC report.

claims.claim: Faster rates of adaptation may be necessary for tropical mosquito populations that already experience environmental temperatures close to their thermal optima.
claims.source: However, while greater warming is projected for higher latitudes (IPCC, 2007), faster rates of adaptation may be necessary for tropical mosquito populations that already experience environmental temperatures close to their thermal optima and may experience large fitness costs under additional warming in the absence of adaptation (Deutsch et al., 2008; Somero, 2010; Ryan et al., 2015; Mordecai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on thermal biology and climate projections, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus are vulnerable to climate warming in their tropical ranges as temperatures are expected to exceed their thermal optima and upper thermal limits in coming decades.
claims.source: For example, although Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus are highly adaptable and have expanded into temperate climates, they are vulnerable to climate warming in their tropical ranges as temperatures here are expected to exceed their thermal optima and upper thermal limits in coming decades (Ryan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claims.claim: There are virtually no estimates of the heritability of thermal tolerance traits, environmental sensitivity of selection, and within-population variation in thermal tolerance for mosquitoes.
claims.source: As outlined above, there are virtually no estimates of the heritability of thermal tolerance traits, environmental sensitivity of selection, and within-population variation (and few estimates of between-population variation) in thermal tolerance for mosquitoes specifically.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of knowledge gaps based on literature review.

claims.claim: Future research should focus on measuring environmental sensitivity of selection, plasticity, and within-population variation and heritability in thermal tolerance.
claims.source: We therefore recommend that future research focus on measuring environmental sensitivity of selection, plasticity, and within-population variation and heritability in thermal tolerance.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the identified knowledge gaps.

claims.claim: Both artificial and natural selection designs have been used extensively with model organisms to measure changes in upper limits of trait thermal tolerance.
claims.source: Both selection designs have been used extensively with model organisms such as Drosophila spp., Daphnia spp., and Escherichia coli to measure changes in upper limits of trait thermal tolerance.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about established methodologies in the field.

results.result: Mosquito demographic characteristics (short generation times and high population growth rates) favor thermal adaptation. The authors synthesize evidence showing that mosquitoes have generation times and growth rates comparable to species that have already demonstrated evolutionary responses to climate change.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C42 provide converging evidence from theory (C35, C36), empirical data on mosquito demographics (C37-C40), and comparative analysis with Drosophila (C41) that collectively support the conclusion that mosquito demographic characteristics favor thermal adaptation (C42). The evidence includes specific quantitative estimates (r = 0.19-0.38, population sizes of 1,000-10,000) and appropriate citations.

results.result: Strong temperature-imposed selection on mosquitoes may facilitate thermal adaptation. Upper thermal limits for mosquito survival are 32-38°C, which many tropical populations already experience, and steep survival declines occur between thermal optima and critical limits.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 provide empirical evidence for strong selection pressure (specific temperature ranges, steep survival declines across species), which supports the theoretical expectation in C58 and the inference in C63. The evidence is well-cited and internally consistent.

results.result: Studies show genetically-based variation in thermal tolerance between mosquito populations, but evidence for local thermal adaptation across climate gradients is inconsistent and unclear. No studies have measured within-population variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 provide a balanced synthesis of the literature showing that while between-population variation exists (C45-C48), the patterns are inconsistent and do not clearly support local adaptation (C49). The assessment of knowledge gaps (C44) and alternative explanations (C50-C51) is appropriately cautious given the mixed evidence.

results.result: There are no estimates of heritability of thermal tolerance for mosquitoes. Evidence from Drosophila suggests moderately low heritability (h² = 0.28), but recent findings challenge this and uncertainty limits extrapolation to mosquitoes.
results.evaluation: The knowledge gap for mosquitoes (C52) is clearly stated. Claims C53-C56 appropriately use Drosophila data with proper caveats, and C57 explicitly acknowledges the limitations of extrapolating from Drosophila to mosquitoes. The synthesis is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Mosquitoes possess various plastic responses to temperature (behavioral thermoregulation, thermal acclimation, dormancy), but the capacity for these responses to increase thermal tolerance, their fitness costs, and interactions with evolutionary adaptation remain poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C80 provide empirical evidence for various plastic responses across multiple mosquito species. However, the synthesis appropriately concludes (C67) that understanding of these mechanisms' effectiveness and interactions with adaptation is limited. The evidence for behavioral thermoregulation is particularly limited (C72), and acclimation effects are minimal (C75-C77).

results.result: Environmental sensitivity of selection has not been empirically measured for mosquitoes. Upper thermal limits are less variable than lower limits across populations and species, which may reflect evolutionary constraints rather than environmental sensitivity.
results.evaluation: The knowledge gap is clearly stated (C82). The empirical pattern (C83) is supported by citations, and the interpretation (C84) appropriately presents multiple possible explanations while acknowledging uncertainty. The speculative nature of the interpretation is appropriately flagged.

results.result: Key knowledge gaps constrain precise estimates of mosquito adaptive potential, including lack of data on within-population variation, heritability, environmental sensitivity of selection, and the role of phenotypic plasticity. Future research should focus on measuring these parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C89 consistently identify the same knowledge gaps, which are well-supported by the detailed review in the manuscript. The recommendation (C91) logically follows from the identified gaps. This represents a synthesis of the major limitations discussed throughout the paper.

results.result: Selection experiments and common garden experiments are established methodologies that can be used to measure key parameters for mosquito thermal adaptation. Several major vector species can be readily maintained in the lab, making these approaches feasible.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C102 describe established methodologies with appropriate citations to examples in mosquitoes and other species. The feasibility for mosquitoes is supported by citations to laboratory methods (C95) and examples of related work (C97, C99). The recommendation (C102) is appropriately framed as a first step.

results.result: Case study: In Northern Brazil, maintaining current dengue transmission suitability under 2080 climate conditions would require the critical thermal maximum of Ae. aegypti fecundity to increase by 1.57°C (0.03°C/year), a rate comparable to evolutionary rates observed in other taxa.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 present modeling results with appropriate context (disease burden, current projections, assumptions). The comparison with other taxa (C116) provides useful context for interpreting the required evolutionary rate. The modeling approach and assumptions are clearly stated (C113), though the result depends on the validity of these assumptions.

results.result: Current predictions of climate impacts on mosquito-borne disease largely ignore adaptive responses and may underestimate future disease risk if mosquitoes adapt to warming temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C107 document the limitation of current modeling approaches, while C18, C109, C117 present the logical inference that adaptation would alter predictions. This is a straightforward inference that follows from the potential for adaptation demonstrated elsewhere in the manuscript.

results.result: The impact of mosquito thermal adaptation on disease transmission is uncertain and could increase, maintain, or decrease transmission depending on the mechanism of adaptation, genetic correlations between traits, and context-specific factors like vector control and pathogen incubation periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C131 present a nuanced discussion of how different adaptive mechanisms could affect disease transmission. The discussion appropriately acknowledges uncertainty (C118, C120, C131) while providing specific examples and mechanisms. The speculative claims are appropriately supported by citations and logical reasoning.

results.result: The evolutionary rescue model has important limitations (lacks genotype-by-environment interactions, evolution in plasticity, gene flow, genetic correlations, and stochasticity), but simulation approaches can incorporate these factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 clearly states model limitations based on the cited theoretical paper. Claims C104-C106 provide examples of how simulations have addressed these limitations in other systems, with appropriate citations. This represents a balanced assessment of the modeling framework.

results.result: Evidence of evolutionary adaptation to contemporary climate change has emerged across diverse taxa, including rapid thermal adaptation in pest species like the European gypsy moth (30 years) and Asian tiger mosquito (10-30 years).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C10, C11 are well-supported by multiple citations to empirical studies. These provide important context for the plausibility of mosquito thermal adaptation by demonstrating that rapid adaptation has occurred in related taxa.

results.result: Mosquito-borne diseases cause ~500 million cases and millions of deaths annually. Temperature is a fundamental driver of transmission, with nonlinear effects on mosquito traits leading to unimodal fitness relationships. Recent forecasts predict decreased transmission in some high-risk areas as temperatures exceed mosquito thermal limits.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 provide well-cited background on mosquito-borne disease burden and temperature effects. These establish the public health importance and scientific context for the study. The claims are appropriately supported by citations to WHO reports and modeling studies.

results.result: Species may respond to warming through range shifts, phenotypic plasticity, or genetic evolutionary adaptation. The focus here is on evolutionary adaptation as it enables in situ persistence and is currently the least well-understood climate response.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 provide clear framing for the study's focus. The rationale for focusing on evolutionary adaptation (C20, C21) is supported by citations and represents a reasonable prioritization given the knowledge gaps.

results.result: Temperature fundamentally limits mosquito ranges through effects on survival, development, and reproduction, but the precise aspects of temperature that determine these limits remain unclear. The limiting temperature variable likely varies by population based on habitat preferences and location.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C29 provide a nuanced discussion of how temperature limits mosquito populations. The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C23) and context-dependence (C25-C26) is appropriate. The inference about maximum temperature (C27-C28) is appropriately cautious, being based on evidence from other arthropods.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that mosquito traits with the lowest critical thermal maxima (adult lifespan and fecundity for several vector species) will experience the strongest thermal selection, though whether these traits pose the strongest constraints on fitness remains poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 presents a clear hypothesis supported by theory and citations. Claim C31 provides supporting evidence from a review paper. Claim C32 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about whether these are indeed the most fitness-relevant traits. This represents a reasonable working hypothesis given current knowledge.

results.result: Evolutionary rescue models, which compare maximum sustainable evolutionary rates to required rates of evolution, are well-suited for estimating thermal adaptation potential in response to climate warming.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 describe the theoretical framework with appropriate citations. The suitability of this approach for the question at hand is supported by citations to applications in other taxa. This provides clear methodological justification.

results.result: Rates of environmental change vary by climate scenario (projections for 2100 vary by >3°C) and location. Faster adaptation rates may be necessary for tropical mosquito populations already near their thermal optima, despite greater warming projected for higher latitudes.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 provide context on climate projections with appropriate citations to IPCC reports and modeling studies. The inference about tropical populations (C87) is well-supported by thermal biology principles and citations. This provides important context for interpreting adaptive potential.

results.result: The framework for investigating mosquito thermal adaptation can be applied to other pest and vector species with similar life history characteristics. Understanding adaptive potential is critical for predicting distributions and informing management strategies under climate change.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C138 appropriately extend the framework to other taxa and discuss practical applications. The example of the European gypsy moth (C134-C136) illustrates the applicability. These claims represent reasonable extensions of the framework, though the actual application to other species would require additional work.

results.result: Synthesis conclusion: Mosquito demographics and strong temperature-imposed selection may facilitate rapid thermal adaptation. Generation times and growth rates are comparable to species showing evolutionary responses to climate change, and steep survival declines and population-level variation indicate necessary selective pressures and genetic material exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 represent the main synthesis conclusions, which are well-supported by the detailed evidence reviewed throughout the manuscript (particularly results 1-5 above). The conclusions are appropriately qualified ('may facilitate') given the knowledge gaps identified.

results.result: Climate change is expected to have major impacts on species distributions, particularly for ectotherms whose traits depend heavily on temperature. Climate change is expected to shift distributions of pest, pathogen, and vector taxa due to nonlinear and interactive effects of temperature and other climatic factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 provide general background on climate change impacts, well-supported by citations to review papers. These establish the broader context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: A general strategy for understanding and estimating climate adaptive potential in pest and vector taxa is lacking.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 represents an assessment of the field that motivates the study. This is supported by the literature review showing scattered evidence but no unified framework, and is consistent with the knowledge gaps identified throughout the manuscript.
